explanations.explanation: This feature is strongly activated by non‐standard, ornamental or placeholder characters—symbols (often rendered as �) that serve to mark stylistic boundaries or signal special formatting/emphasis in otherwise “normal” text. When the feature is active, these unusual glyphs appear instead of ordinary tokens (e.g. “the” or “-”), indicating that the model distinguishes and treats these formatting or encoding markers differently from typical language tokens.

This feature appears to detect non‐semantic “marker” tokens—special symbols or placeholders that demarcate a shift in content (for example, as used for formatting, linking, or indicating missing/annotated data). In short, it signals boundaries or transitions in the text’s structure rather than conveying conventional linguistic meaning.

It’s a feature that signals a morphological “split‐or‐join” decision at subword boundaries—in other words, it biases the model to complete a word with the correct affix or ending (and when removed, a different, “contrapositive” suffix appears).

It appears that this feature “lights up” on text segments that serve as formal, structured metadata – the kind of language found in citations, technical specifications, publication details, and other official document or reference information.

It appears that this feature “lights up” on markers that signal a hard boundary in the text—in practice, sentence‐ending punctuation or a clear discourse break. In other words, the feature encodes the transition point (typically marked by a period or similar token) that tells the model “this thought is complete” so that if it weren’t active the model might instead continue in a “contrapositive” or alternate direction.

This feature appears to signal when a period functions as a marker for a sentence (or segment) boundary—typically at the end of an abbreviation or proper noun—thereby cueing the model to expect a capitalized or structurally distinct token soon after.

It’s a detector for concrete numeric specification details—tokens (and adjacent segments) that mark measurements, counts, sizes, and other product‐ or property–specification numbers and units in descriptive or technical text.

explanations.explanation: It appears that this feature is acting as a signal for sentence‐termination and the ensuing discourse break. In other words, it’s highly activated at end‐of-sentence punctuation (or similar boundary markers), thereby shifting the model’s next-token prediction to ones appropriate for a new sentence (often starting with a pronoun like “I,” “to,” etc.).

It’s a marker for abbreviated, “initial‐style” punctuation—that is, the feature fires on periods that follow a single (or very short) token (e.g. an initial in a name or a shorthand label) and cues the model to expect the next token to continue that proper‐noun or structured formatting pattern.

It “lights up” on unusual sub‐word pieces—bits of names, loanwords, or marked morphemes (often including non‐standard, accented or special characters) that occur at atypical token boundaries in proper names or foreign/compound words. In other words, the feature detects and marks fragments with distinctive orthography that signal a break in a multi‐token entity.

It appears that the feature “lights up” on the beginnings of celebratory, achievement‐oriented, or promotional announcements. In other words, it detects when text is introducing or highlighting accolades, awards, or other success events (often via token fragments or prefixes like “Cong,” “Hyp,” or “Lead”) that signal an announcement of achievement or celebratory flair.

It picks out when the text is talking about an entity’s temporal “origin” or duration—that is, it fires on phrases that mark when something was established or describe a time span (using “founded” or “purchased” in dates, “year,” “week,” “long,” etc.) and thereby helps guide the right grammatical choices (for example, “founded in” rather than “founded on”).

It appears this feature is sensitive to particular subword “end‐markers” – the affix or terminal fragment in a compound or proper noun – that cue the model into a specialized, often technical or named‐entity usage. In short, it detects and propagates morphological endings (or similar internal splits) that signal brand names, compound adjectives, or proper noun fragments, thereby influencing the downstream token prediction.
It’s a punctuation‐detection signal that fires on period tokens used as abbreviation markers (in names, acronyms, or similar shortened phrases) rather than sentence–final periods.

It’s a marker for templated, boilerplate content—an internal “formatting cue” that fires when the model is generating or recognizing automatically produced, placeholder‐style text (such as autogenerated landing pages, standardized ad or review copy, etc.) that uses a special symbol and fixed phrasing.

It detects when the text uses a non‐standard “marker” – a decorative or delimiter glyph (or series of them) inserted into otherwise ordinary text to set off, emphasize, or partition content. In other words, this feature flags those atypical, visually “special” symbol tokens that serve as stylistic or formatting signals.

It’s a detector for sentence‐or sentence‐fragment–ending punctuation—a signal that a complete, self‐contained unit (often in lists, ads, or announcements) has just ended, and the following token will begin a new segment.

It’s a feature that fires on non–word‐initial, “continuation” subword pieces—that is, parts of a multi–token word (often in names, specialized terms, or foreign/compound expressions) that serve as suffixes or internal fragments. In short, it signals that the token is not a full independent word but the trailing segment of one.

explanations.explanation: It’s a subword‐level “name/term preservation” signal—that is, a feature which kicks in on fragments (often with diacritics or unusual letter groupings) found in proper names, technical terms, or foreign-language text, biasing the model to choose the precise, less “normalized” token split versus a more generic, altered alternative.

It appears that this feature “lights up” at discourse‐boundaries—especially at sentence– or clause–end markers and at tokens that initiate shifts in topic or style. In short, it signals a break or transition in the text structure that nudges the model’s next–token distribution toward choices typical of ending a thought or beginning a new section.

It’s a detector for a particular “suffix‐oriented” subword unit—that is, it fires on short word endings (or joiner fragments) that routinely occur as the second part of compound or morphologically complex words (in names, technical terms, hyphenated expressions, etc.) and thereby signal a shift in token–prediction.

It’s a marker‐feature that lights up when the text contains nonstandard, “placeholder” or extra‐formatting characters (often rendered as � and similar glyphs) that usually occur in technical or reference-style material (e.g. bibliographic entries, license texts, mixed‐language or formulaic strings). In short, it detects injected formatting or noisy punctuation used to segment or signal structured metadata in the source text.

It appears that the feature is sensitive to a particular morphological‐boundary signal—in practice, it “lights up” when a word ending in the professional or technical suffix “-ists” is generated rather than the root “-ist.” In other words, it detects the pluralized form (and related token splits) of specialist/scientific terms, which are common in academic, technical, and scientific discourse.

This feature signals when the model encounters a period‐based punctuation marker—typically at abbreviated or sentence‐terminating points—which cues a syntactic or formatting boundary and thus shifts the distribution for the following token.

explanations.explanation: It’s a feature that flags sentence‐ or clause–final punctuation boundaries—activating strongly on terminal markers (like periods) to signal the end of a structured segment in text.

It appears this feature “lights up” when a token is an internal sub‐word or name fragment—that is, a piece that routinely appears mid–word in compound names or multi‐part terms (often from foreign or complex morphology, as in “Rapunzel,” “Van der …”, “McMenamin,” “cul‑de‑sacs,” etc.). In effect, the feature signals that the token is not a standalone word but a bound segment helping to form a larger, structured proper noun or compound term.

It appears to be a metalinguistic “clarification‐and‐explanation” signal—a feature that, when active, pushes the model toward words that foreground a reflective, evaluative, or definition‐seeking mode (for example, explicitly asking “what does … mean?” or “reviewing” a claim) rather than a more straightforward, “matter-of‐fact” continuation.

It activates on boilerplate, system‐generated meta text—that is, text signaling a templated or automatically created page (or entry) with standardized metadata (e.g. “placeholder page,” “posted,” “automatically”) that cues predictable continuations.

It appears to be a feature that “lights up” on the sub‐word boundary elements—especially those created by hyphenation or split affixes in multi‐token names or compound words. In other words, it detects when a word is broken into parts (or “joined” via a dash or similar fragment) and marks those linking or fragmental morphemes that help build compound or proper‐noun tokens.

This feature signals when a token is part of a hyphenated (or otherwise joined) compound modifier. In other words, it activates on and helps generate compound constructions—whether standard compound adjectives (like “hassle‑free”, “hands‑on”, “bite‑sized”, “shrink‑wrapped”) or similar joined forms—ensuring that the second part of the compound is produced in the proper context.

This feature appears to function as a subword‐segmentation or continuation “switch” that, in context, decides between alternative endings of a multi‐piece word. In the examples it lights up on the intra‐word fragments of items like “Gävle,” “Golden Nugget,” “gummy bears” and even in contractions like “haven’t.” In short, its activation encodes a learned preference for one specific token completion (one morphemic or subword segmentation) over an alternative, effectively controlling how the model “glues” together or splits apart words under different contexts.

explanations.explanation: This feature appears to fire when the model is in a “compositional‐linking” or “material specification” mode. In contexts ranging from product description to technical or even metaphorical language, it cues the connective element (often a short function word or morpheme such as “of,” “from,” or a compound‐split element) that links an item’s quality, composition, or component to the thing being described.

It picks out a specific, high‐information subword fragment—that is, a common morpheme or “word‐piece” usually found at a boundary (often the beginning) of a compound or proper noun—that carries a distinctive semantic or stylistic “core.” In other words, the feature fires when a token contains a salient, decomposable fragment (like “Mar” in “Marcos,” “orge” in “gorgeous,” or “and” in “tandems”) whose removal leaves a different, less‐informative remainder.

It appears that the feature “lights up” when the text shifts into an illustrative or descriptive mode—that is, when the speaker signals an example, comparison, or depiction (using cues such as “like,” “how,” or “mean”) to show what something looks or “sounds” like.

It activates on tokens that signal formal abbreviated names or acronyms—instances where a period is used as part of an institutional or title abbreviation (e.g. “Gov.” or “U.” in “U.S.”) in news‐style or official text.

It’s a “paired‐choice” or slash‐mechanism feature—that is, a latent signal that marks tokens as part of a dual or compound construction (e.g. his/her, HIV/AIDS, TCP/IP, GNU/Linux, etc.) and biases the prediction toward the second (often context‐specific or stylistically preferred) alternative in such paired, slash‐ or hyphen‐separated expressions.

It detects when “high” is being used as an intensifier in compound phrases—that is, it cues a continuation where “high‐” modifies a noun (e.g. “altitude,” “pass,” “risk,” “calorie,” “rise,” etc.) to denote an extreme or elevated quality.

explanations.explanation: It is a feature that detects compound or morphologically split expressions—signaling when a subword or hyphenated fragment is part of a multi‐word phrase—and thereby biases the model to complete the idiom or compound in a semantically coherent way.

It fires when the model “recognizes” a name‐fragment—a distinctive proper‐noun stem that cues a well‐formed entity (a company, person, brand, etc.)—so that its presence steers the completion toward the expected, idiosyncratic spelling of that proper name rather than an alternate ending.

It appears that this feature is picking up on negation‐oriented “switches” – the moments when a clause is being negated or otherwise limited, canceled, or qualified. In the examples the model boosts tokens like “wouldn’t,” “cannot,” “not,” and related words, which then shift the choice of following determiners or pronouns. In short, the feature encodes a negation or cancellation concept that helps steer the generation of tokens in contexts where the meaning is being reversed or constrained.

It signals that the model is at a sentence‐ or clause–boundary marked by terminal punctuation. In other words, this feature activates when a period (or similar punctuation) demarcates the end of a formal textual unit, thereby cueing a shift in style and context for the following tokens.

It is detecting compound word constructions—especially ones joined by a hyphen or similar split—where two morphemes combine (like “life‐threatening,” “ex‐girlfriend,” “short‐hairstyles”) to form a modifier or semantic unit.

It appears this feature encodes a boundary‐signal – a strong marker for sentence or segment endings (typically a period) that signals a complete, self‐contained unit and steers the choice of the following token.
It flags language used to express positive evaluation or endorsement—words and phrases that indicate a recommendation, support, or favorable descriptive assessment.

It’s a feature that detects “how‐to” question phrases—in other words, it signals when the context is asking for an instruction or procedure (as in “How to …”) and guides the model toward the expected continuation of a procedure rather than an unrelated token.

This feature appears to be tracking a syntactic “slot‐filler” signal—that is, it lights up when the context calls for a particular type of function word (or morpheme) to introduce an upcoming noun phrase or complement. In many examples it biases the prediction toward an indefinite “a” (versus “the”), or a structural preposition like “into” or “from”, thereby ensuring the following phrase fits the expected grammatical construction.

It detects a structured numeric “fraction‐style” pattern—that is, a whole number immediately paired via a slash with a following number to express a measurement or mixed numeral (as in “1 1/2” or “1/4”) in descriptive, specification‐type text.

This feature appears to detect a syntactic decision point in directive or instructive contexts where an infinitive marker (“to”) is preferred over a clausal complement (“that”). In other words, it signals that the upcoming phrase should be structured as an action or instruction (infinitival construction) rather than a statement or subordinate clause.

It encodes a punctuation‐boundary signal—especially around abbreviated or terminal punctuation—that cues the model a sentence or segment has just ended and thus changes the expected form (e.g. capitalization or style) of the following token.
